 Ryzen 5800X3D Revival was Lisa Su's Initiative, and Other Interesting Details in AMD Interview with MyNavi Tech+ 
 by btarunr 
 Today, 05:19
 Discuss (13 Comments) 
 Japanese tech publication MyNavi Tech+ interviewed Travis Kirsch, the client-segment product manager for AMD, and there are some interesting excerpts from the conversation. It turns out that reviving Ryzen 7 5800X3D for the Socket AM4 market earlier this year, was an initiative going as far up as CEO Lisa Su. The effort required certain manufacturing process updates with TSMC to ensure they can build new 5800X3D chips that are identical in specs to the original ones, without having to revive deprecated manufacturing processes. 
AMD says that 5800X3D AM4 Anniversary Edition was released as a parting gift to the loyal Socket AM4 crowd that's holding on to DDR4 memory in the wake of brutal overpricing of DDR5. It was planned to help users better plan their transition to AM5 and DDR5 memory. The 5800X3D offers contemporary levels of performance with games, and its re-launch triggered a new wave of product launches from motherboard vendors. Next up, AMD was quizzed on why it decided to launch the Ryzen 7 7700X3D based on the slightly older "Zen 4" microarchitecture instead of the "Ryzen 7 9700X3D" positioned below the 9800X3D and 9850X3D. The company said that it wanted to use up its volumes of "Raphael" chips. Launching a "9700X3D" would've meant eating into the common stock of "Granite Ridge" chips meant for higher 9850X3D SKUs.
When asked to comment on the state of the memory market, Kirsch said that the current situation with the memory pricing is beyond anyone's control, and AMD has to respond to market realities ensuring consumers get an AMD-powered PC regardless of the price-point. The company still has an active Socket AM4 product line, including the top performing 5800X3D. 
Tech+ then steered towards the juicy topic of why AMD isn't offering entry-level Ryzen 3 SKUs, leaving Intel uncontested in that segment, to which AMD responded that the component market for Ryzen 3 is "small," and that the focus for the company is premium gaming. 
Lastly, AMD confirmed that the upcoming "Zen 6" microarchitecture will continue to see a common CCD being shared between consumer and enterprise products, and the company's strategy remains unchanged in this regard. Having a common CCD lets AMD build these chiplets at scale and dynamically allocate them between vastly diverse product lines.

 mrnagant 
 Paganstomp Release a CPU for an old platform to get around a RAM shortage which put more pressure on the previous generation supply.
Motherboard suppliers started cranking out new AM4 boards with the idea of making a quick buck using up resources and components for newer platforms.
I'm not convinced if that was a good strategy. Small components isn't the issue. It's storage based stuff. You have machines and cleanrooms that are already geared for DDR4 production. Not all of these are DDR5 and not all of them will or can get converted to DDR5. So releasing something that needs DDR4 won't impact DDR5. 
Keeping AM4 around longer would only impact DDR5 if DDR4 and DDR5 where manufactured side by side using the same exact equipment. The problem is AM4 will keep the more limited supply of DDR4 demand high which impacts prices of DDR4. But it is still half the cost of DDR5. 
It's like the difference between building something on 2nm vs building something on 16nm. Those 16nm machines can't make 2nm chips. So coming out with chips on 16nm won't impact 2nm supply. Designing and building on 16nm though when you can, actually helps 2nm supply by keeping those on an older production node.
